passages.title: Allah's absolute oneness and self-sufficiency declared
passages.tafsir:
These four short ayat — the whole of Sūrah al-Ikhlāṣ — are the Qur'an's most concentrated statement of who Allah is: One, needed by all and needing none, without parent, child, or equal. The sources record that the sūrah came down in answer to people who demanded to know about Allah's lineage — though the reports differ over exactly who asked — and the four ayat move in one unbroken line: ayah 1 affirms Allah's absolute oneness, ayah 2 His self-sufficiency, and ayat 3–4 strip away every false comparison — lineage, offspring, or peer — that people have ever attached to Him.

## The question that brought it down

Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad, on the authority of Ubayy bin Ka'b, that the idolators came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Muhammad! Tell us the lineage of your Lord." In answer, Allah revealed this sūrah. At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir recorded a similar report, and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded it; At-Tirmidhi noted a *mursal* (disconnected) version of it and judged that to be the most correct. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays the account, from At-Tirmidhi, Al-Hakim and others, that it was the pagans of Makkah who asked, while some narrations ascribe the question to the Jews of Madinah — and in some reports the questioners went further, asking whether Allah was made of gold, silver, or some other stuff. Because of these differing accounts, the scholars differed over whether the sūrah is Makkan or Madinan: Ibn Mas'ud, Hasan al-Basri, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Jabir held it Makkan, while Qatadah, Dahhak and others held it Madinan, with both views reported from Ibn 'Abbas (as al-Qurtubi relays).

'Ikrimah widens the frame further, as Ibn Kathir cites: the Jews said "We worship 'Uzayr, the son of Allah," the Christians said "We worship the Messiah, the son of Allah," the Zoroastrians said "We worship the sun and the moon," and the idolators said "We worship idols" — and against all of them Allah revealed, "Say: He is Allah, One."

Notice how the question is answered. They asked about Allah's ancestry; the reply does not give Allah a family tree — it announces that He is above any such thing. Ayah 3, "He begets not, nor was He begotten," is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the direct response to those who questioned about the ancestry of Allah: there is no analogy between the Creator and His creation — creation comes into being through procreation; Allah has no children and is the child of no one.

## Ayah 1: why "Aḥad" and not simply "One"

The command *qul* ("Say") is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to it: the very imperative marks him as Allah's Messenger, charged to convey this message to mankind. "Allah," it explains, is the personal name of the Necessary Being — the One whose non-existence is inconceivable — who possesses every attribute of perfection and is above every imperfection.

Then comes the key word: *Aḥad*. Arabic has two words commonly rendered "One": *wāḥid* and *aḥad*, and both are applied to Allah. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *aḥad* carries an extra charge: it signifies that Allah is beyond composition, plurality, and resemblance — He is not assembled from parts or elements, has no partner, and resembles nothing. That is precisely the answer to those who asked whether He was made of gold, silver, or pearls. Ibn Kathir adds that *al-Aḥad* cannot truly be affirmed of anyone except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because only He is perfect in all His attributes and actions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān remarks that this one brief sentence, properly analysed, contains the detailed discussions of entire volumes of theology.

## Ayah 2: aṣ-Ṣamad — needed by all, needing none

*Aṣ-Ṣamad* is a name so rich that, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the exegetes assigned it several meanings. Tabarani gathered all the interpretations of this divine attribute in his Kitāb us-Sunnah and concluded that they are all authentic and together comprehend the attributes of our Lord — but that the root sense is "the chief who has no superior, to whom people turn for the fulfilment of their needs; all depend on him while he depends on no one."

The early authorities cited by Ibn Kathir fill this out. Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of 'Ikrimah, said it means "the One Whom all of creation depends upon for their needs and their requests." In the report of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, Ibn 'Abbas expanded it into a litany of perfection: the Master perfect in His sovereignty, the Most Noble perfect in His nobility, the Most Magnificent perfect in His magnificence, the Most Forbearing perfect in His forbearance, the All-Knowing perfect in His knowledge, the Most Wise perfect in His wisdom — attributes befitting none but Allah, who has no coequal and nothing like Him. And Abu Wa'il said simply: aṣ-Ṣamad is "the Master Whose control is complete."

In the narration of At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir mentioned above, an explanation of aṣ-Ṣamad is given that ties ayah 2 directly to ayah 3: aṣ-Ṣamad is the One who does not give birth and was not born, "because there is nothing born except that it will die, and nothing dies except that it leaves behind inheritance — and Allah does not die and leaves no inheritance." Birth, death, and inheritance form one chain of dependency; aṣ-Ṣamad stands entirely outside it.

## Ayat 3–4: no child, no parent, no equal

"He begets not, nor was He begotten" (ayah 3) means, as Ibn Kathir states plainly, that He has no child, no parent, and no spouse. Mujahid explained "there is none comparable to Him" (ayah 4) as "He does not have a spouse" — for offspring presuppose a partner. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. How can He have children when He has no wife? He created all things" (6:101). He who owns and created everything can have no peer among His creatures, and no relative who resembles Him. Ibn Kathir also cites Allah's severe words about those who ascribe a son to Ar-Raḥmān — "the heavens are almost torn apart" at the claim, for "there is none in the heavens and the earth but comes unto Ar-Raḥmān as a slave" (19:88–95). He cites too Allah's declaration that those whom people called Ar-Raḥmān's offspring "are but honored servants. They speak not until He has spoken, and they act on His command" (21:26–27), and His words against those who "have invented a kinship between Him and the Jinn" — "Glorified is Allah from what they attribute unto Him!" (37:158–159).

Two hadith in Sahih Al-Bukhari show how gravely Allah Himself speaks of this claim — and how patiently. In one, the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no one more patient with something harmful that he hears than Allah. They attribute a son to Him, while it is He Who gives them sustenance and cures them." In the other, from Abu Hurayrah, Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: "The Son of Adam denies Me and he has no right to do so, and he abuses Me and he has no right to do so… As for his cursing Me, it is his saying: 'Allah has taken a son.' But I am the One, the Self-Sufficient Master. I do not give birth, nor was I born, and there is none comparable to Me." The wording of the sūrah itself is placed on Allah's own tongue as His answer to the insult.

For ayah 4, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks *kufuwan*: an "example," a "similar thing," "one equal in rank and position." The verse therefore means that no one in the entire universe is, ever was, or ever can be similar to Allah, equal to Him in rank, or resembling Him in His attributes, works, and powers in any degree whatsoever. Ayah 4 thus closes the circle opened by ayah 1: *Aḥad* at the start, "no *aḥad* comparable to Him" at the end.

## One sūrah, every false belief answered

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the four ayat together into a map of every way people have gone wrong about Allah. Some deny His existence altogether; some grant His existence but deny it is necessary; some grant both but deny His attributes of perfection; some grant all this yet worship many gods. Ayah 1 — He is Allah, the Necessary Being, One — refutes all of these at a stroke. Ayah 2 addresses a subtler error: those who worship Allah alone yet believe other helpers can fulfil their needs — aṣ-Ṣamad denounces any such notion, for all needs return to Him alone. And ayah 3, *lam yalid*, repudiates in the strongest terms those who ascribe children to Him. The sūrah is thus, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān titles it, a comprehensive lesson in Allah's oneness and a complete negation of shirk (associating partners with Allah) in all its forms.

## "A third of the Qur'an": what the Prophet ﷺ said about this sūrah

Ibn Kathir devotes pages to the virtues the Sunnah attaches to these four ayat.

**Equivalent to a third of the Qur'an.** Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Sa'id that a man heard another repeating "Say: He is Allah, One" over and over through the night and mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ, as though belittling it. He ﷺ said: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul, verily it is equivalent to a third of the Qur'an." (Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i also recorded it.) In another hadith Al-Bukhari alone recorded, also from Abu Sa'id, the Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions, "Is one of you not able to recite a third of the Qur'an in a single night?" — and when they found this daunting, he said: "'Allah is the One, aṣ-Ṣamad' is a third of the Qur'an."

**Love of it leads to Paradise.** Al-Bukhari reported (with Muslim and An-Nasa'i) from 'A'ishah that a commander of an expedition used to close his recitation in prayer with this sūrah; asked why, he said, "Because it is the description of Ar-Raḥmān, and I love to recite it." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Inform him that Allah the Most High loves him." Al-Bukhari also recorded (with a disconnected chain, but in a manner indicating his approval) the story of the imam of Masjid Quba' who began every rak'ah with it; when he told the Prophet ﷺ "Verily, I love it," he ﷺ replied: "Your love of it will cause you to enter Paradise." And Imam Malik recorded from Abu Hurayrah that when the Prophet ﷺ heard a man reciting it he said, "It is obligatory." Asked what was obligatory, he said: "Paradise." At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i also recorded it, and At-Tirmidhi graded it "Hasan Sahih Gharib" — the scholars' technical terms for a report he judged sound (*hasan sahih*) yet rare in its route of transmission (*gharib*); as he himself explained, "We do not know of it except as a narration of Malik."

**A daily protection.** In a hadith recorded by Abdullah bin Imam Ahmad — also by Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi (who again graded it "Hasan Sahih Gharib") and An-Nasa'i — the Prophet ﷺ taught a Companion to recite "Say: He is Allah, One" together with the two sūrahs of refuge (al-Falaq and an-Nās) three times each, morning and evening: "They will be sufficient for you two times every day," and in An-Nasa'i's wording, "They will suffice you against everything." Al-Bukhari likewise recorded from 'A'ishah that every night at bed the Prophet ﷺ would cup his palms, blow into them, recite these three sūrahs into them, and wipe over his head, face, and the front of his body, three times.

**Allah's greatest Name.** An-Nasa'i recorded in his Book of Tafsir, from 'Abdullah bin Buraydah, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ heard a man supplicating with the meanings of this sūrah — "You are the One, the Self-Sufficient Sustainer of all, Who does not give birth, nor were You born, and there is none comparable to Him" — and said: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul, verily he has asked Him by His Greatest Name… if He is asked by it, He will give, and if He is called upon by it, He will answer." (At-Tirmidhi graded it "Hasan Gharib" — sound, but transmitted through a rare route.)

## Living with these ayat

The sources themselves sketch the practice: recite this sūrah in prayer out of love for it, as "the description of Ar-Raḥmān"; recite it with the two sūrahs of refuge morning, evening, and at bed as a shield; and turn its words into supplication, calling on Allah as al-Aḥad, aṣ-Ṣamad. Underneath the practice lies the creed: because He is aṣ-Ṣamad, every need — sustenance, cure, help — is brought to Him and to no one besides Him; and because none is comparable to Him, nothing in creation may be given the devotion that is His alone. Four short ayat, and the Prophet ﷺ weighed them as a third of the Qur'an.
